title: Under his wings (Psalm 91)
hook: he shall cover you with his feathers

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses' prayer and a life worth counting. Your line was number our days. What was the one thing from yesterday you'd want to keep? Day four hundred twenty-nine.

A shadow crosses the farmyard. A hawk, circling low. The hen doesn't run. She makes one sharp sound, and every chick within earshot comes skittering across the dirt and disappears under her. In two seconds there's no chick to be seen, only a hen who suddenly looks twice her size, feathers puffed, eyes on the sky. Underneath, it's warm and dark and loud with heartbeats. People who keep chickens see it often. The writers of the Bible had seen it too, and they used it for God. Today, Psalm ninety-one, a psalm said at night, and the picture of being hidden under wings.
screen: `A HAWK'S SHADOW.` → `THE HEN CALLS.` → `NO CHICKS IN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: The psalm opens, in the King James Bible: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty." Then, verse four: "He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust." The Hebrew word for wing is kanaf. It also means the edge of a cloak. In the book of Ruth, Boaz blesses Ruth, the foreigner who has come to Israel, as one who has come to trust under the wings of the God of Israel. Later, at night, Ruth asks Boaz to spread his kanaf, his cloak, over her, and the King James Bible translates it skirt. Wings and a cloak: both are ways of saying you're covered, you belong. The psalm goes on: "Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day." That is one reason it belongs to the night. It is part of Jewish bedtime prayers, and some churches pray it at Compline, the last service of the day. But the psalm can be misused. In the Gospels, when the devil tempts Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple, he quotes this very psalm: he shall give his angels charge over thee. Go on, jump. And Jesus answers, "It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." The psalm is a place to hide, not a dare to take. And Jesus used the same farmyard picture himself, over Jerusalem: how often would I have gathered thy children together, "even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings."
screen: `COVERED WITH HIS FEATHERS` · `KANAF: A WING, A CLOAK'S EDGE` · `NO TERROR BY NIGHT` · `A SHELTER, NOT A DARE` · then, large: `UNDER HIS WINGS SHALT THOU TRUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for protection for someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who could use covering right now. Someone traveling, someone sick, someone scared, a kid walking into a hard week. Picture them clearly: where they are, what they're facing. If you pray, you can ask God to cover them with his feathers, in the psalm's own words, or simply say their name to God and leave it there. If you don't pray, hold them in mind and wish them safe, steadily, the way a hen sits still. The bell holds the time.
Under his wings. Psalm ninety-one's picture of God as a bird sheltering its young, a psalm for the night.
Your line: under his wings. Tonight, as the lights go off, name one person you'd want sheltered, and keep them in mind as you fall asleep. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Psalm 91 is a night psalm for many Christians: it is prayed at Compline in Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran traditions, and many people pray it for protection before travel, surgery or military service.

original.note: Hebrew: wing, and also the corner or edge of a garment.

trapdoor: what you thought: a promise that nothing bad will ever happen to believers.
what it means: a night prayer about shelter and trust, which even Jesus refused to turn into a dare.
what a scholar hears: kanaf means wing and cloak's edge; Ruth is blessed under God's wings and asks Boaz to spread his kanaf over her.

notes: Ruth 2:12 (KJV 'under whose wings thou art come to trust') and Ruth 3:9 (KJV 'spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid', Hebrew kanaf). Confirm.
Jewish use: Psalm 91 is part of the bedtime Shema in many Jewish prayer books. Christian use: Compline (Roman Sunday Compline; Anglican and Lutheran orders). Confirm.
'He shall give his angels charge over thee' (Psalm 91:11; Matthew 4:6) is spoken without quotation marks in the script, as a paraphrase.
The farmyard hook is a general description of hen behavior; confirm it reads as accurate.
